Each stone is carefully cut and ground, and its natural grain is kept so as to preserve the tone. The instrument has a wooden hanging frame, usually of hardwood, for stability and durability. It is struck with a wooden or bamboo mallet whose head is often wrapped in leather or cloth to adjust the timbre. The body of the stone is hollowed inside to strengthen the resonance.

Its range is fairly wide and its pitches are clearly separated; struck, it gives a sustained, pleasing sound. Its resonance is unusual: the sound wave travels directly through the stone itself, producing a pure and penetrating sound in which the timbre carries little harmonic clutter. Set against the metallic feel of bronze percussion, the stone chime sounds softer and more contained; set against the xylophone, its sound carries further and lasts longer. Striking different points gives different colours, and the whole sound has the elegance of ancient East Asian music. It is often used to create a still, far-reaching mood, and it is an important source of colour for traditional court music and for contemporary composition.

The stone chime is an important percussion instrument of ancient China, dating from the Neolithic, eight thousand years ago. It is made of natural stone or jade, shaped as a chime stone, and usually hung on a wooden frame. Its timbre is crisp and bright, with the warm smoothness of jade; struck, the sound wave travels directly through the stone and produces a pure, penetrating sound. In the Shang and Zhou periods it became an important instrument of court sacrifice and ritual music, and later it was widely used in folk music and temple music, often together with the bianzhong (bronze bell chimes).
石磬起源於中國新石器時代，最早的石製打擊樂器遺跡可追溯至距今八千年前。它在商周時: Stone chimes originated in Neolithic China; the earliest traces of a struck stone instrument go back eight thousand years. They were widely used in the Shang and Zhou periods and became an important instrument of court sacrifice and ritual. They are usually made of natural stone or jade, and struck they give a crisp, pleasing sound.
站於琴前，雙手持棒敲擊琴鍵中央。手持樂器本體，透過敲擊、搖晃、刮奏或撥彈等方式使: Stand at the instrument and strike the centre of the bars with a stick in each hand. Take the instrument itself in your hands and set it vibrating by striking, shaking, scraping or plucking; different parts and different amounts of force give different timbres. Begin by settling into the correct hold on the instrument, and once the basic way of sounding it is secure, work on rhythm patterns and melodies. Strike the surface with a finger or a drumstick and let the rebound lift it naturally, keeping the wrist loose.

It is still regarded as a classic representative of traditional Chinese instruments.
